title: The Minus-Times-Minus Mystery
intro: You've seen the pattern. Today it forces the answer.

blocks.html:
At the dinner table you met this pattern:

3 × −6 = −18
2 × −6 = −12
1 × −6 = −6
0 × −6 = 0
−1 × −6 = ?

Look at the answers: −18, −12, −6, 0… they're climbing by 6 every line. The pattern doesn't care what we think should happen next. It just keeps climbing.

blocks.prompt: Follow the pattern one more step each time:
blocks.hint: The answers climb by 6 each line: −6, 0, then… keep climbing.

blocks.html:
The pattern says minus times minus is positive — and the debt story agrees.

−4 × −6 means: take away four debts of £6.

Every debt removed makes you £6 richer. Remove four of them and you're £24 richer: +24.

So the rule isn't a rule at all. It's two facts pointing the same way:

minus × plus = minus (four debts of £6 = −£24)
minus × minus = plus (removing them = +£24)

blocks.prompt: The rematch — this exact question beat you on the diagnostic. Not today:
blocks.hint: Minus times minus is plus. Then 4 × 6.

blocks.prompt: Mixed signs — check the sign first, then multiply:
blocks.hint: Different signs → negative answer. Same signs → positive answer.

blocks.html:
Division is just multiplication in reverse, so the same sign facts hold:

(−24) ÷ (−6): what times −6 makes −24? It's 4 — same signs, positive.

18 ÷ (−3): what times −3 makes 18? It's −6 — different signs, negative.

blocks.hint: Same signs → positive. Different signs → negative.

blocks.prompt: Boss move. Three negatives walk into a bar: (−2) × (−3) × (−4)
blocks.hint: Do it two at a time: (−2) × (−3) first — that's positive. Then × (−4).

blocks.html:
🏔️ For the dinner table: people say “two wrongs don't make a right” — but in maths, two minuses do make a plus. Explain to Dad, using debts, why removing debts makes you richer.

Then the sting in the tail: why did three minuses in the boss question make a minus again? What would four make? Is there a pattern for any number of minuses?

done.title: Mystery solved ✓
done.html:
Negatives: added, subtracted, multiplied and divided. That's the entire Year 7 directed-numbers toolkit, and you built the hardest rule yourself from a pattern.
